html:
The Ramcharitmanas, "Lake of the Deeds of Rama", is a retelling of the Ramayana in Awadhi, an eastern form of Hindi. The poet Tulsidas began it at Ayodhya in 1574 and finished it at Varanasi some years later. It is the most widely read book in north India.

The Sanskrit epic could be read only by the learned. Tulsidas put the story into the language of farmers, in verses made to be sung. Tradition says the Brahmins of Varanasi opposed him for it.

His Rama is God, and the poem is an act of devotion. Its message is that love of Rama and the saying of his name are enough to save anyone. It belongs to the bhakti movement, in the same years that Akbar ruled at Agra. Tulsidas lived to a great age and died at Varanasi in 1623.

Its reach is hard to overstate. Villagers who could not read knew long passages by heart. The Ramlila, the play of Rama's life acted each autumn in thousands of towns, uses its words. The Hanuman Chalisa, forty verses to Hanuman also credited to Tulsidas, is recited daily by millions. Workers shipped overseas under indenture carried the book to Fiji, Mauritius and Trinidad.
